newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Further Spanish rate cut this year.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Further Spanish rate cut this year.

text.p: The Bank of Spain has room for a further 25 to 50 basis point cut in its key money market rate, on the basis of the ample spread between the Spanish and German repo rates and moderate inflation expectations, analysts said.
"I think we'll see at least another 50 (basis point cut) over the next three months," Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
Nevertheless, it was unlikely another rate cut would come through before December when the next few months' inflation data will be known.
The Bank of Spain is expected to a take a breather after Thursday's 50 basis point rate cut, which brought the repo rate down to a historic low of 6.75 percent.
"Another rate cut is unthinkable from now for the next eight regular tenders (around 2-1/2 months), except if the Bundesbank cuts rates," said the treasury chief at a large Spanish bank.
But the German central bank was unlikely to ease again before the end of the year, traders said, leaving the Bank of Spain to focus on domestic concerns.

"For the Bank of Spain, the most important objective is inflation and we will at least have to see the data from September and October (due to be released on October 11 and November 14 respectively) before starting to think reasonably about a new rate cut," the treasury chief said.

The government aims to bring inflation down to 3.4 percent this year. August's lower-than-expected rate of 3.7 percent has sustained hopes that the official target will be met despite a rise in some taxes such as those on alcohol and cigarettes.
The inflation target for 1997 is 2.6 percent.
"All available data indicate the inflation objectives can be met," said Segura Porta, head of research and strategic planning at Caja de Catalunya.

A report by Banco Central Hispano (BCH) said factors in favour of another rate cut included positive inflation expectations, peseta strength, falling import prices, moderating monetary aggregates and lack of demand pressures.
It expects the money market rate to fall to 6.50 percent by the end of 1996.

Analysts said the central bank could also take advantage of the spread between the Spanish and German repo rates, which at 375 basis points was ample compared with the spread between 10-year Spanish bonds and German Bunds of 173 basis points.

"The differential between the German and Spanish repo rates gives the Bank of Spain margin for another rate cut this year," said Segura Porta. "I think the cautious thing would be to look for a quarter-point (cut) and optimistically speaking, we could get up to a half-point."
The Bank of Spain has cut rates six times this year from 9.00 percent in January.
